Want to move more? Start with what is near you. Badminton, running, cycling or swimming can all work if you want to return next week.
Studies or official product pages linked
Check for convenient places first, then consider time and cost. Pick a sport your body tolerates and you want to repeat. Start this week.

A means strong guidance or consistent research. B means useful research exists, but your own result remains uncertain. C means evidence comes mainly from related activities, with little direct evidence. Each letter applies to the claim on that card.
Find one you want to keep doing
If you have a partner, try badminton. Prefer solo time? Try running or cycling. Access, cost and comfort all count.
If a court and partner are nearby, arrange a game. Equipment and court time cost money; what matters is whether you will want to play regularly.
A UK study grouped badminton, tennis and squash and found lower all-cause mortality among participants. A Danish study separately found an estimated life-expectancy difference for badminton players.
These figures do not mean badminton adds years to your life. Health and living conditions may differ between groups; adapt if your knees or ankles hurt.
Watts et al. · JAMA Network Open (2022)
Schnohr et al. · Mayo Clinic Proceedings (2018)
Start by alternating running and walking. Choose a safe route, keep an easy pace, then build your time slowly.
Long-term studies found lower all-cause mortality among runners. In one US older-adult study, the running group had about 15% lower mortality risk than the comparison group.
That is a group difference, not a promise for you. Sudden increases invite injury; ease off with persistent pain.
Watts et al. · JAMA Network Open (2022)
Already have a bike and a safe route? Try a short ride. A commute or relaxed ride counts; no new gear is needed to begin.
A UK study found lower all-cause mortality among cyclists. US and later studies found weaker or mixed results.
Include bike cost, upkeep and road safety. Do not force a ride through unsafe traffic to meet a target.
Watts et al. · JAMA Network Open (2022)
If you can swim and have a safe pool nearby, swimming can be a form of aerobic movement you enjoy.
A UK study observed lower all-cause mortality among swimmers; another long-term study did not find a clear difference.
Results differ. Consider pool fees, travel and water safety.
Watts et al. · JAMA Network Open (2022)
Start with a free guided session or a community class. Finding a format you want to repeat is a good first step.
UK and US cohort studies found lower all-cause mortality among people who joined aerobics and related activities.
Those studies grouped many styles and intensities. They cannot show that one class or routine works better.
Watts et al. · JAMA Network Open (2022)
No room to swing a rope? Use ropeless handles, or simply turn your wrists and make small jumps. Try a short bout first, check your landing space and balance, then build up gradually.

The American Heart Association lists jumping rope as aerobic exercise, and WHO recommends regular activity. These sources concern activity in general or skipping with a rope; long-term evidence for the ropeless version is limited.
Removing the rope does not remove landing impact or noise. If your knees or ankles hurt, balance is difficult, or noise is a concern, choose walking or another activity.
Town et al. · Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise (1980)
Take one or two flights when it feels safe and comfortable. Stop when you need to; there is no pace to beat.
A long-term study found lower all-cause mortality among people who climbed stairs. Everyday stair climbing counts as movement.
Choose another activity if your knees hurt, you feel dizzy or falling is a concern. Stairs do not replace all aerobic and strength work.
Walk, break up sitting, and try one leg, one pushing and one pulling movement. Aim for strength work on at least two days a week.
Start with a ten-minute brisk walk
Walk part of an errand or get off transit one stop early. Breathing a little harder while still able to talk is a simple starting pace.
WHO recommends adults build up 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week and says some movement is better than none.
You do not need to reach that range in your first week. Increase gradually and adjust if something hurts.
Use a sturdy chair. Plant your feet, stand up from sitting, then lower yourself slowly. Use the chair for support if needed and reduce support as you gain control.
WHO recommends strengthening major muscle groups on at least two days a week. The NHS uses chair stands as a leg-strengthening movement.
Ease off or stop if your knees or hips hurt, you feel dizzy, or balance is poor. Legs alone do not cover the whole body.
Face a wall with hands at shoulder height. Bend your elbows to move toward it, then push back. Start with a number you can control.
The NHS lists wall push-ups as an upper-body strengthening movement. Pair them with a leg exercise.
Adjust your distance or stop if your wrists or shoulders hurt. Keep breathing as you move.
Secure a light resistance band, sit or stand, pull it toward your body and release slowly. Begin with gentle resistance.
The NHS uses band rows for back and arm work. WHO recommends strength work across the major muscle groups.
Check the anchor and band for damage before pulling to avoid snapback. Stop if your shoulder or back hurts.
Get up after sitting for a while
After a long stretch at a desk or on your phone, walk a little, get water or stretch.
WHO advises less sedentary time. Replacing some sitting with light movement can help.
There is no proven minute-by-minute timer. Standing briefly does not replace regular exercise.
After trying it, vote to tell other readers whether you would recommend it.

Stop and seek medical advice if exercise brings chest pain or marked dizziness. Ask a qualified professional before starting if you have heart disease, pregnancy-related limits or another restriction.
